passage: The manager wanted the payments feature within a fortnight. Payal did not answer from a feeling. She listed every task with the hours it needed and added them up: it came to six weeks. With those figures in hand, she did not just say no. She went back with three choices: everything in six weeks, the main flow in a fortnight with money matched by hand, or a working prototype in a fortnight. The manager chose the main flow. Imran, a junior lead in another team, was given a similar deadline and said yes on the spot, without checking the numbers. He worked until midnight for days, quality slipped, and bugs reached the live system. His manager took away only one lesson: the timeline had been fine, so the next one would be tight as well. Vandana ran into a delay from a supplier halfway through her own project. She told her manager the same day, shared a new date and proposed handing one task to a different team, so nobody was surprised in the last week.

qa.q: How many weeks did Payal's task list add up to?
qa.a: Payal's list added up to six weeks.

qa.q: How does Imran's answer to his deadline differ from Payal's, and what happened as a result?
qa.a: Imran said yes without checking and worked nights, so quality fell and bugs went live. Payal counted the hours and offered three options, and the manager chose the main flow.

qa.q: What was Imran probably feeling when he said yes on the spot?
qa.a: He was probably anxious to please and afraid of seeming unable, so he agreed before checking.

qa.q: What could Imran do the next time he is handed a tight deadline?
qa.a: He could list the tasks with rough hours and take a few options to his manager, as Payal did. A clear estimate makes it easier to talk about what fits. 🙂

grounding: Four professionals answer an unrealistic deadline by estimating, offering scope options, silently accepting, and flagging a risk early.
